title: 5 Signs You Are Harboring Elephants In Your Meeting Rooms
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain opens with a dramatized staff meeting in which the room goes quiet, nobody names any problem, and the real talk resumes the moment the leader leaves. He argues that this pattern means unnamed elephants are not just ignored but nurtured and growing. He offers five telltale signs: conversations skirting the real issue, recurring agenda topics, body language that contradicts words, the meeting after the meeting at the watercooler, and superficial or stalled decisions. Each sign comes with a concrete leader script such as naming the pattern or reconnecting a decision to purpose. He closes with a one-liner to use in the next meeting: what is the one thing we are avoiding talking about today.
points: A silent room when the leader asks for hot topics is evidence of a culture where problems are being avoided rather than a sign that nothing is wrong.
Euphemisms such as optimizing expenses in place of naming a budget shortfall show a conversation staying in the safe zone.
A topic that returns three meetings in a row is a symptom of unwillingness or inability to decide, to be named directly and given a deadline.
Side conversations at the watercooler indicate people do not trust the meeting space to handle debate productively.
Weak agreement can signal misalignment on the why, so decisions should be reconnected to purpose before they are finalized.
quotes: I argue that there are one or more elephants in the room, who are not just being ignored, but simultaneously being nurtured, and they’re growing with every passing moment.
The discussion dances around the real problem, circling it like a shark but never going in for the bite.
If a topic has been on the agenda for three meetings in a row, it’s no longer just an “item”, it’s a symptom. It’s a sign that your team is either unwilling or unable to make a decision.
When key debates happen outside the main discussion, it’s usually because people don’t trust the meeting space to handle them productively.
This often happens when there’s a deeper misalignment on the “Why.” Without shared purpose, decisions lack energy.
As much as you may like elephants, you can’t afford to harbor them in your meeting rooms. Mind you, the more you ignore them, the bigger they’ll grow.
